title: throttLL'eM: Predictive GPU Throttling for Energy Efficient LLM Inference Serving
problem: LLM inference serving on GPUs consumes excessive energy while providers must simultaneously satisfy Service-Level Objectives (SLOs); static GPU frequency settings over-provision compute resources when request load is low or KV cache pressure is manageable.
method: throttLL'eM uses instance sizing and GPU frequency scaling guided by an ML model that predicts future KV cache usage and batch size. The ML model receives projections of these metrics as inputs and outputs per-iteration performance estimates, enabling iteration-level frequency decisions. The R^2 score exceeds 0.97 and misprediction is under 1 iteration/second on average. Frequency scaling and instance count adjustments are applied jointly to reduce energy while keeping within SLO bounds.

title: Using Analytical Performance/Power Model and Fine-Grained DVFS to Enhance AI Accelerator Energy Efficiency
problem: DVFS on AI processors has historically been applied at coarse granularity (entire program or sub-phases) because the control latency of DVFS mechanisms exceeds the duration of individual AI operators, leaving per-operator energy optimization unexploited. This coarse-grained DVFS fails to match voltage/frequency to the actual compute intensity of each AI operator.
method: The paper proposes an analytical performance/power model that characterizes the compute- and memory-boundedness of individual AI operators, enabling prediction of which operators tolerate voltage/frequency reduction without performance loss. Combined with a hardware mechanism to reduce DVFS control latency, the system applies fine-grained DVFS at the AI-operator level: memory-bound operators run at lower frequency while compute-bound operators run at peak frequency, minimizing energy waste during memory-stall phases.

title: Delinquent Loop Pre-execution Using Predicated Helper Threads
problem: Helper-thread branch pre-execution fails when delinquent branches are control-dependent on other delinquent branches: prior work must branch-predict the first delinquent branch (b1) in the helper thread to decide whether to pre-execute the second (b2), merely shifting the misprediction bottleneck to the helper thread. Additionally, stores that both influence a delinquent branch and are control-dependent on it create a disambiguation problem in helper threads.
method: Phelps (Predicated Helper Threads) constructs a helper thread for each inner loop containing delinquent branches and unconditionally pre-executes all delinquent branches (including control-dependent ones) in every loop iteration. Per-branch queues are managed in lockstep with loop iterations, so the main thread can correctly consume or ignore b2 outcomes based on b1 results. Influential stores that are control-dependent on delinquent branches are predicated on those branch outcomes in the helper thread. A dual decoupled helper thread scheme handles outer-inner loop pairs with short/unpredictable inner-loop trip counts.

title: Gaze into the Pattern: Characterizing Spatial Patterns with Internal Temporal Correlations for Hardware Prefetching
problem: Existing spatial-region hardware prefetchers predict memory access footprints using system-level context features (trigger PC, data address) that fail to capture the intrinsic characteristics of spatial access patterns, resulting in poor flexibility and suboptimal prefetch accuracy across diverse workloads.
method: Gaze extracts footprint-internal temporal correlations — the ordering and timing relationships among cache line accesses within a spatial region — as the primary feature for characterizing and predicting spatial access patterns. This avoids dependence on trigger PC or address-based context lookup. For spatial streaming patterns (very high access density within a region), Gaze applies a dedicated two-stage prefetch approach to suppress over-prefetching: a first stage filters high-density streaming footprints and a second stage applies targeted prefetch decisions to avoid redundant prefetches.

title: In-Storage Acceleration of Retrieval Augmented Generation as a Service
problem: As RAG deployments shift knowledge bases to persistent NVMe storage to handle ever-growing corpora, the Search & Retrieval phase — comprising embedding model inference, similarity/relevance search over dynamic data structures, and long-latency storage accesses — becomes the dominant bottleneck for end-to-end latency.
method: The paper proposes a metamorphic in-storage accelerator architecture embedded within NVMe storage devices. The in-storage accelerator is programmable to support diverse RAG retrieval algorithms, dynamic data structures (e.g., HNSW, IVF), and varying computational patterns. It executes smaller language models for query embedding generation entirely in-storage, while the final LLM generation runs on DGX A100 systems. The metamorphic design adapts its functional units to the retrieval algorithm at hand without requiring host CPU involvement in the hot path.

title: COMET: Towards Practical W4A4KV4 LLMs Serving
problem: Prevalent LLM quantization methods (W8A8 or W4-only) do not fully utilize INT4 tensor cores on modern GPUs and cannot reduce the KV cache memory bottleneck, because quantizing activations to 4-bit causes unacceptable accuracy loss with standard methods, leaving W4A4 impractical.
method: COMET introduces a fine-grained mixed-precision quantization algorithm (FMPQ) that compresses most activations to 4-bit while preserving accuracy by identifying and retaining outlier activations at higher precision (e.g., 8-bit) in a mixed-precision format. On the hardware side, COMET develops a highly optimized W4Ax GPU kernel (supporting both W4A4 and W4A8 mixed-precision GEMM) with a novel mixed-precision data layout that co-locates 4-bit and 8-bit activation elements to enable fast dequantization. The kernel uses GPU software pipelining to overlap data loading and conversion with computation, and introduces fine-grained streaming multiprocessor (SM) scheduling to achieve load balance across SMs. COMET integrates this kernel into a full LLM inference framework with efficient KV4 cache management supporting models like LLaMA-3-70B on a single A100-80G.

title: Enhancing Large-Scale AI Training Efficiency: The C4 Solution for Real-Time Anomaly Detection and Communication Optimization
problem: Large-scale distributed LLM training across thousands of GPUs suffers from efficiency loss due to (1) hardware failures that are slow to detect and isolate, and (2) network traffic collisions that cause prolonged GPU idle time during collective communication synchronization steps.
method: C4 exploits two properties of distributed training workloads: (1) homogeneous, iteration-structured load means hardware anomalies produce detectable syndromes in collective communication patterns, enabling rapid faulty-component identification, isolation, and task restart without waiting for software-level timeouts; (2) collective communication involves a small number of long-lived, predictable flows, allowing C4 to perform proactive traffic planning that eliminates bandwidth contention among these flows and reduces collision-induced queuing.

title: TidalMesh: Topology-Driven AllReduce Collective Communication for Mesh Topology
problem: Existing AllReduce algorithms are topology-aware adaptations of generic algorithms (ring, tree) to physical 2D mesh networks, resulting in a mismatch between logical and physical communication patterns that wastes bandwidth and increases latency.
method: TidalMesh is a topology-driven AllReduce algorithm designed natively for 2D mesh networks. It pushes data flows between endpoint nodes in a wave-like (tidal) pattern that aligns with the mesh grid structure, fully utilizing bidirectional links and minimizing congestion. Sparse TidalMesh minimizes the bandwidth overhead of the base algorithm. Collective communication unrolling enables software pipelining by superimposing different AllReduce phases (ReduceScatter, AllGather) so that compute and communication overlap across multiple concurrent AllReduce operations, effectively hiding collective communication latency.

title: EOD: Enabling Low Latency GNN Inference via Near-Memory Concatenate Aggregation
problem: Real-time GNN inference for online services requires an inductive setup where the system must first prepare the computational graph and node features before executing inference, with this preparation step dominating end-to-end latency. The neighborhood explosion problem causes exponential growth in memory access and computation as the number of GNN layers increases.
method: EOD co-designs algorithm and hardware to tackle both challenges. On the algorithmic side, it introduces a precomputation method for training nodes that converts exponential neighborhood aggregation to linear complexity, and a concatenated Zero-Value Compression (ZVC) scheme to compact the stored precomputed hidden features. On the hardware side, EOD implements a Near-Memory Processing (NMP) architecture that performs aggregation directly on ZVC-compressed, concatenated feature data without decompressing to host memory, exploiting the high internal memory bandwidth to eliminate the PCIe/host-memory bottleneck during the preparation stage.

title: Prosperity: Accelerating Spiking Neural Networks via Product Sparsity
problem: Existing SNN accelerators exploit bit sparsity (zero-valued spikes) to skip zero multiplications, but this approach leaves substantial redundancy unexploited: non-zero spike patterns that produce structurally identical inner products across matrix rows are recomputed independently, wasting significant compute.
method: Product Sparsity is a new sparsity paradigm that identifies combinatorially similar binary spike patterns across matrix rows: if two rows share identical non-zero positions, their dot products with the same weight vector are identical and only one needs to be computed, with the result reused for the other. Prosperity implements this via a real-time pattern matching engine that groups rows by their spike pattern hash, computes the inner product once per unique pattern, and distributes results to all matching rows. This is applied to both fully-connected and convolutional layers of SNNs with binary activations.

title: Predicting DRAM-Caused Risky VMs in Large-Scale Clouds
problem: DRAM failures in large-scale clouds are currently mitigated at node granularity, requiring migration of all VMs on a node even when errors affect only a small fraction of the memory address space. This coarse-grained approach consumes excessive resources and causes unnecessary VM disruptions.
method: Pegasus introduces an Error-VM mapping framework that correlates DRAM ECC error addresses to specific VM memory regions using address space management metadata. A predictor combines ECC correction event features with spatio-temporal clustering features to identify VMs whose working sets overlap with DRAM regions exhibiting uncorrectable error risk. The system operates at VM granularity rather than DIMM/node granularity, enabling selective migration of only at-risk VMs.

title: HyperHammer: Breaking Free from KVM-Enforced Isolation
problem: Existing Rowhammer attacks against virtualized cloud environments can compromise co-resident VMs but have not demonstrated the ability to attack the hypervisor itself, and a key primitive enabling such attacks (double-sided hammering or similar) has been disabled by hypervisor mitigations. This paper develops a new Rowhammer attack capable of breaking KVM-enforced isolation to compromise the hypervisor from a guest VM.
method: HyperHammer constructs a new Rowhammer attack path from within a KVM guest VM that circumvents existing KVM-level mitigations. The attack likely leverages alternative hammering primitives or physical memory addressing techniques (e.g., virtual-to-physical mapping exploitation, huge-page-based addressing) to induce bit flips in hypervisor memory regions, enabling privilege escalation from guest to hypervisor level.

title: Harmonia: A Unified Framework for Heterogeneous FPGA Acceleration in the Cloud
problem: The shell-role FPGA architecture adopted by cloud providers works well for homogeneous FPGA servers but fails to handle heterogeneous FPGA configurations: prior solutions either require laborious shell development for each FPGA variant (provider burden) or ad-hoc software modifications for each application (user burden), with no portable abstraction across diverse cloud FPGA types.
method: Harmonia introduces a unified framework that abstracts cloud FPGA heterogeneity at both the hardware and software levels. On the hardware side, it defines a standardized shell interface specification that decouples platform-specific shell logic from portable role logic, allowing roles (user accelerators) to be written once and ported across heterogeneous FPGAs. On the software side, Harmonia provides a resource management layer and a driver abstraction that hides FPGA-specific differences from user applications, enabling portability without per-FPGA software modifications.

title: PartIR: Composing SPMD Partitioning Strategies for Machine Learning
problem: Training large neural networks requires combining multiple parallelization strategies (data, model, and optimizer sharding), but existing systems make it difficult to compose, verify, and reason about these strategies in a predictable way. The tight coupling of partitioning strategies with ML implementation code makes it hard to experiment with or automatically derive optimal sharding plans.
method: PartIR provides a schedule-like API that incrementally rewrites a neural network's intermediate representation (IR) after each applied partitioning strategy. Each strategy (data parallelism, tensor/model parallelism, optimizer sharding) is expressed as a composable, declarative transformation on the IR. The system is hardware-and-runtime agnostic and follows well-defined general rewriting rules so each step is independently verifiable. Simulators and users can check the strategy's effect after each incremental rewrite.

title: A Probabilistic Perspective on Tiling Sparse Tensor Algebra
problem: Tiling sparse tensor algebra computations for cache efficiency is challenging because the effective tile size and cache behavior depend on the sparse data distribution, which varies across inputs and is not known at compile time.
method: The paper takes a probabilistic approach to sparse tensor tiling, modeling the sparsity pattern probabilistically to predict cache behavior and guide tile-size selection. Specific mechanism details are not available from the abstract alone.

title: Architecting Value Prediction around In-Order Execution
problem: In-order processors suffer from stalls when long-latency instructions block younger independent instructions from issuing, and the compiler cannot always find sufficient independent work to fill the pipeline. Conventional branch prediction techniques fail to resolve hard-to-predict (delinquent) branches quickly enough to prevent pipeline bubbles.
method: The paper integrates both address-based value prediction and direct value prediction into an in-order pipeline (based on a scaled-up CVA6 RISC-V core), exploiting the property that in-order execution allows aggressive value speculation without recovery penalties (a mispredicted value simply overwrites its slot when the real result arrives). A reworked cache hierarchy adds a fast first-level cache that can be written speculatively. A 32-entry scoreboard 4-issue in-order pipeline is augmented without full register renaming or out-of-order memory hazard handling.
